provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court vacated and remanded, holding that before a State may irrevocably sever the parent-child relationship the Due Process Clause requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, so a preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: The federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof in every Pennsylvania involuntary termination case.
key_cases.quote: the "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard prescribed by Fam. Ct. Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

key_cases.holding: The court reversed and ordered termination of parental rights for five siblings, holding that under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(b) an unhealthy or pathological parent-child bond does not preclude termination and that courts must weigh the child's need for permanency and any bond with a pre-adoptive family.
key_cases.relevance: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare analysis and the weight of parent-child bonds at termination.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that severing the parental bond best serves the needs and welfare of these children

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating termination, the court held that incarceration is not itself a ground for termination but may be determinative of parental incapacity under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(a)(2), with the length of the remaining sentence highly relevant.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Pennsylvania rule on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent.
key_cases.quote: incarceration, while not a litmus test for termination, can be determinative of the question of whether a parent is incapable of providing "essential parental care, control or subsistence"

key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that appellate courts must review sua sponte whether the orphans' court appointed counsel for the child's legal interests under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a), but may not assess sua sponte the quality of that representation or an unraised conflict.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling rule on the child's right to appointed legal counsel in a contested termination and how that right is policed on appeal.
key_cases.quote: we hold that appellate courts should engage in sua sponte review to determine if orphans' courts have appointed counsel to represent the legal interests of children in contested termination proceedings

key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that a child's statutory right to appointed counsel under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a) cannot be waived, but that where the child is too young to express a preferred outcome the attorney-guardian ad litem may represent both legal and best interests without conflict.
key_cases.relevance: Defines who must speak for the child at termination and when a single attorney may serve both roles.
key_cases.quote: we hold that a child's statutory right to appointed counsel under Section 2313(a) of the Adoption Act is not subject to waiver

key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court affirmed termination and held that a parent's claim of ineffective assistance in a termination proceeding is reviewed on direct appeal under a fundamental-fairness standard, with relief only where counsel's failure caused the decree.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the Pennsylvania right to counsel in involuntary termination and what a parent must show to upset a decree on that ground.
key_cases.quote: Mere assertion of ineffectiveness of counsel is not the basis of a remand or rehearing

key_cases.holding: Vacating the orders below and remanding, the court held that a 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare analysis may not stop at evidence of an emotional or adverse-impact bond but must determine whether the parental bond is necessary and beneficial and must also weigh the child's need for permanency, stability and any bond with a pre-adoptive family.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling modern Pennsylvania statement of the § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare and bond analysis, decided a decade after T.S.M. and correcting the truncated reading lower courts had drawn from it.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, to grant termination when a parental bond exists, there must be clear and convincing evidence that the bond is not necessary and beneficial.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and remanding with instructions to reinstate the trial court's order, the court held that the Superior Court exceeded its scope of review in rejecting supported findings that the father's alcoholism was an obstacle he overcame with reasonable firmness, and that the petitioners proved neither § 2511(a)(1) nor § 2511(a)(2) by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the § 2511(a)(1) abandonment ground, the petitioner's clear-and-convincing burden, and the deference an appellate court owes the trial court's findings on parental duties.
key_cases.quote: In recognition of the gravity attendant to the termination of parental rights, the moving party must establish the statutory grounds by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and remanding for a new termination proceeding, the court held that 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a) requires appointment of counsel to serve the child's legal interests in a contested involuntary termination, and that the failure to appoint such counsel is structural error not subject to harmless-error analysis.
key_cases.relevance: The origin of the § 2313(a) separate-counsel and structural-error rule that In re T.S. and In re Adoption of K.M.G. build on; Parts I, II(A) and II(C), which contain both holdings, are the Opinion of the Court even though Part II(B) commanded only a plurality.
key_cases.quote: we hold that Section 2313(a) requires the appointment of counsel who serves the child's legal interests in contested, involuntary TPR proceedings.

state_agency.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth, and Families

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21, conditional: adjudicated dependent before 18, youth requests the court to retain jurisdiction, and meets one of five activity conditions; re-entry may be requested before 21 (42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6302, 6351(j))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
